label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court confirmed that the August 8, 1952 lease deed fixed the tenancy for one year rather than creating a monthly tenancy. Lines L80-L83 establish the duration of the relevant lease, and L89 confirms that the first appellate court erroneously treated the appellant as a monthly tenant. Although L51-L52 alone do not expressly specify the duration of the 1952 lease, the subsequent judicial findings establish the proposed connection.

original_spans.original: It is, therefore, manifest that the lease was for a period of one year and that it was not a monthly tenancy.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The High Court held that the tenancy had expired by efflux of time and that no termination notice was consequently necessary. The Supreme Court independently confirmed that the fixed one-year term had expired and that the appellant was not entitled to statutory notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. This supports R4.P2 for the particular expired fixed-term tenancy. It does not establish that the actual notice complied with section 106 or remove the separate protection afforded by section 13 of the Rent Control Act.

original_spans.original: As the term fixed under the deed had expired, the appellant was not entitled to any statutory notice

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court expressly recorded that the appellant had sublet rooms after the 1952 lease without obtaining the landlord's written consent. Section 13(1)(b)(i) applies to unauthorized subletting of the whole or any part of the premises after the Act's commencement. The Court applied that provision to the established subletting and rejected the appellant's argument that replacement occupants were outside its scope. The proposal correctly identifies the operative subletting ground, although the judgment does not give individual dates for the new subtenancies.

original_spans.original: Here, admittedly after the lease deed of 1952 the appellant has sublet some of the rooms of the building to others without obtaining the written consent of the landlord.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The absence of written landlord consent is expressly established by the Supreme Court's account of the appellant's subletting. Section 13(1)(b)(i) specifically requires written consent for the covered disposition. The Court concluded that the appellant could not invoke section 13 protection because he had sublet part of the premises without that consent. This supports R2.P3 and the proposed connection when read together with the established subletting event; absence of consent alone would not establish every element of the statutory exception.

original_spans.original: The appellant, having sub-let part of the premises without the consent of the landlord in writing, cannot invoke the protection given to him

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court directly found that earlier subtenancies had terminated and that the appellant himself inducted the new subtenants. The new occupants did not derive their occupation from the earlier subtenants. The Court expressly rejected the contention that replacing an earlier subtenant necessarily escaped section 13(1)(b)(i). Accordingly, the proposed connection supports R3.P1 and the characterization of the appellant's conduct as fresh subletting rather than a legally exempt substitution. The source does not establish a universal rule about all conceivable replacement arrangements.

original_spans.original: the new sub-tenants were not holding under the earlier sub-tenants, but were inducted by the appellant, after the earlier sub-tenancies were terminated.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The High Court reversed the first appellate decision on the basis that the tenancy had expired by efflux of time. The Supreme Court expressly identified the first appellate court's contrary treatment of the appellant as a monthly tenant, despite the lease deed's fixed term, as an erroneous legal basis for refusing eviction. It further held that the resulting decree was not according to law and that section 35 authorized the High Court's intervention. This establishes R5.P2. The precise assessment that the decree was not according to law is the Supreme Court's express reasoning in L89, rather than a separately reproduced statement from the High Court.

original_spans.original: the Civil Judge refused to pass an order of eviction on a wrong legal basis that the appellant was a monthly tenant, ignoring the express term in the lease deed itself.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court's procedural account establishes that the landlord obtained an ejectment decree against Ram Saran Das on January 30, 1959. The Court expressly concluded that this decree terminated the main tenancy before commencement of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. This directly supports R5.P1. The conclusion is grounded in the Supreme Court's appellate judgment, rather than an independently reproduced trial-court finding.

original_spans.original: The landlord by obtaining a decree for eviction against the 2nd respondent put an end to the tenancy before the commencement of the Act.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court expressly recorded that Ram Kishan Das was not a party to the ejectment proceedings against Ram Saran Das. It further determined that the decree did not terminate the sub-tenancy because the sub-tenant's rights had not been put in issue. These findings directly support R5.P2 concerning the survival of the sub-tenancy interest following determination of the main tenancy. The cited evidence establishes survival of that interest without independently adjudicating every condition for statutory direct tenancy.

original_spans.original: The Sub-tenancy of the 1st respondent was not determined by the decree

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed connection incorrectly infers lawful subletting from the existence of a tenancy relationship and an ejectment decree against the main tenant. The Supreme Court identified Ram Saran Das as the tenant and Ram Kishan Das as a sub-tenant, but those facts do not independently establish that the premises were lawfully sublet for purposes of section 18(2). Although lawful subletting is a statutory condition, the judgment does not separately present evidence or an adjudication conclusively resolving that condition. The proposed inference therefore upgrades an established tenancy relationship into an unsupported affirmative finding of lawful subletting. This does not establish that the subletting was unlawful.

original_spans.original: Ram Saran Das, res- pondent No. 2 herein, was the tenant of the appellant in respect of the said premises and Ram Kishan Das, respondent No. 1 herein, was a sub-tenant.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court expressly adopted an alternative analysis under section 20 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952. It explained that eviction of the main tenant caused the sub-tenant to be deemed a tenant directly under the landlord. Applying that reasoning to the January 30, 1959 ejectment decree, the Court concluded that Ram Kishan Das had acquired a vested right before commencement of the 1958 Act. This directly supports R7.P1 as an adopted appellate legal conclusion. The Court's conclusion does not require an independently established date of completed physical dispossession.

original_spans.original: He had therefore acquired a vested right under the Act of 1952.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court stated that no provision of the 1958 Act had been identified to it as extinguishing the vested right acquired under the earlier legislation. This supports R7.P2, whose premise is specifically framed around the absence of an identified divesting provision. The connection is valid within that scope. The Court's language should not be expanded into an independently demonstrated, exhaustive conclusion concerning every conceivable legal mechanism for extinguishing vested rights.

original_spans.original: No provision of the Act has been pointed Out to us which took way that right.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court expressly concluded that the 1958 Act contained no provision empowering the Rent Controller to determine a dispute concerning Ram Kishan Das's particular vested right under the earlier legislation. This directly supports R7.P3. The Court used this absence of specialist jurisdiction to explain why section 50 did not exclude civil-court jurisdiction over the claimed pre-existing right. The finding concerns that specific vested-right dispute and does not establish that the Controller lacks jurisdiction over every sub-tenancy dispute.

original_spans.original: There was also no provision under the Act empowering the Controler to decide a dispute raised in regard to the said right vested in the 1st respondent.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed opposition does not identify a genuine contradiction. R5.P1 concerns whether the main tenancy was determined before commencement of the 1958 Act. R6.P1 concerns whether the same pre-commencement ejectment decree could also trigger a vested tenancy right under section 20 of the earlier legislation. These are compatible legal consequences of the same historical event. The Supreme Court expressly relied on the January 30, 1959 decree both to establish pre-commencement termination for section 18(2) and to recognize a vested right under the earlier Act. The alternative statutory analysis reinforces rather than opposes the relevant temporal premise. The distinction between the two statutory routes therefore cannot support the proposed opposition.

original_spans.original: The appellant obtained a decree for eviction against the 2nd respondent on January 30, 1959. cite12†The Act came into force subsequently.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The source confirms that the Supreme Court rejected the Full Bench's view that default under section 15(1) automatically entitled the landlord to possession. However, the Supreme Court agreed that the Controller could not extend the statutory payment period. More importantly, R06.P1 concerns the factual failure of Hem Chand to comply with the section 15(1) order, not the Full Bench's legal assertion about automatic eviction. The recorded late payment and subsequent failure to deposit rent monthly support the factual default rather than oppose it. The proposed connection therefore conflates disagreement over the legal consequences of default with opposition to the factual premise itself.

original_spans.original: The arrears were not paid within a month

label: UNRESOLVED
basis: The Supreme Court expressly stated that the High Court should have considered whether the Rent Controller properly struck out Hem Chand's defence. This establishes that the earlier High Court proceedings did not resolve that issue. However, R08.P1 specifically concerns the High Court's determination on remand, not a determination already made before the Supreme Court judgment. The source contains the Supreme Court's remand instructions but no subsequent High Court decision. Consequently, the proposed opposition correctly identifies the absence of an earlier determination but cannot establish whether the remand-stage premise was ultimately satisfied or contradicted. The later determination remains unresolved within the supplied source.

original_spans.original: The High Court ought to have considered and decided in the appeal whether the striking out of the defence by the Rent Controller was right or not.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court gave a conditional direction: if the High Court subsequently found that the Rent Controller had erroneously struck out the defence, the case would return to the Rent Controller for fresh disposal after hearing the parties. Allowing Hem Chand's appeal and remitting the landlord's appeals to the High Court did not establish that this condition was satisfied. The proposal improperly converts a conditional instruction into an actual finding of error. It also misidentifies the decision-maker: the Additional Rent Controller struck out the defence, whereas the High Court was required to review the propriety of that action. The supplied judgment does not establish that the High Court found the striking-out order erroneous.

original_spans.original: But in the event of the High Court holding that the order of the Rent Controller striking out the defence was erroneous, it will remit the matter to the Rent Controller for fresh disposal, after hearing the parties.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 accurately reports the ARC's finding that no inference of subletting or parting with possession by Mohan Lal in favour of Anand Parkash could be drawn. The High Court expressly confirmed that the ARC's reasoning was based on its assessment of oral and documentary evidence. This supports R1.P1 as an evidence-based first-instance factual determination. The ARCT's subsequent contrary finding does not negate the evidentiary character of the ARC's original determination.

original_spans.original: This reasoning arrived at by the ARC was a sound reasoning

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed direction is OPPOSE, but the cited records support rather than oppose R1.P2. Record 2 reproduces the ARCT's conclusion that Mohan Lal assigned tenancy rights and parted with possession. Record 3 reproduces the High Court's determination that the ARCT's contrary conclusion was manifestly perverse. The High Court expressly stated that the Tribunal reappreciated oral and documentary evidence, reversed the ARC's finding without plausible reason, and reached a conclusion inconsistent with its preceding discussion. These passages substantiate the premise of an unjustified appellate factual reversal. They cannot establish the proposed opposition relationship. The ARCT's ultimate dismissal of the eviction petition on inheritance grounds does not change this assessment of its intermediate factual conclusion.

original_spans.original: The RCT has reversed this finding for no plausible reason

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 describes the ARC's determination concerning alleged parting with possession by Mohan Lal. Its characterization is consistent with the express first-instance finding that deceased Mohan Lal was the tenant. The High Court independently confirmed that the tenancy was in Mohan Lal's name and that he had originally rented the premises for his son's business. Accordingly, the connection supports R5.P1 concerning Mohan Lal's original tenancy identity. It does not establish that Anand Parkash became the original contractual tenant merely because he operated a business there.

original_spans.original: the tenancy although was in the name of Mohan Lal

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 genuinely supports the original-letting and known-use facts: the ARC found that Mohan Lal rented the premises for Anand Parkash's business and that the landlord knew Anand had used them from the beginning. The High Court confirmed these facts through the landlord's cross-examination. However, the proposed connection expressly attributes this establishment to Records 1 and 4 together. Record 4 is a passage quoted from the separate Ram Sarup decision concerning a purported subtenant's inheritance of tenancy during pending proceedings. It does not establish the original letting purpose, the landlord's contemporaneous knowledge, or Anand Parkash's continuous use in the present case. Treating that precedent passage as additional case-specific factual evidence incorrectly transfers its statement status and scope. Therefore, the proposed combined record connection is unsupported as written, although the underlying R5.P2 facts are independently supported by Record 1 and other passages in the judgment.

original_spans.original: The alleged sub-tenant has become, a tenant in his own right during the pendency of the proceedings.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Neither Record 1 nor Record 4 states that rent receipts were maintained in Mohan Lal's name or signed by Anand Parkash on his behalf. Record 1 concerns the ARC's rejection of an inference of subletting based on original business use and landlord knowledge. Record 4 quotes the Ram Sarup inheritance reasoning from a separate decision. Consequently, the proposed statement that these two records show the rent-receipt evidence is inaccurate. The underlying proposition of continuing supervisory control is nevertheless supported elsewhere in the judgment: the documentary-evidence discussion describes the rent-receipt counterfoils, and the High Court expressly found that Mohan Lal retained complete supervisory control. This independent support does not repair the incorrect attribution of that evidence to Records 1 and 4.

original_spans.original: it is apparent that he had complete supervisory control over this business

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The underlying identification of Sh. Surender Kumar as the original tenant is supported by the petitioner's pleading and the trial court's finding. However, the proposed connection incorrectly attributes Record 1 to the petitioner. Record 1 is the respondent's counsel's submission at L100, not the petitioner's allegation. The petitioner's actual allegation appears at L70, and the court confirms the tenant's identity at L118. Although the substantive premise is supported, the proposed connection is not supported with its stated record attribution and procedural status.

original_spans.original: On the other hand it is submitted by the counsel for respondent that premises was let out to the respondent no.1 in his personal capacity

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The court's finding in Record 2 supports opposition to R1.P2: Balaji Enterprises was found to be the original tenant's sole-proprietorship concern, and possession remained with that tenant. PW-3's testimony also supports common proprietorship, although PW-1 denied that Surender Kumar owned Balaji Enterprises. Nevertheless, the proposed connection inaccurately describes Record 1 as the petitioner's allegation of subletting. Record 1 is the respondent's counsel's submission denying subletting or parting with possession. The petitioner's actual allegation appears at L73 and L109. Consequently, the substantive opposition is supported, but the proposed connection as written contains an incorrect party and record attribution.

original_spans.original: Even after creation of new firm possession of the tenanted premises is with the original tenant.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The proposed contextual connection is supported within the scope of the trial court's disposition. In Record 2, the court found that the original tenant retained possession notwithstanding the creation of Balaji Enterprises. In Record 3, the court consequently rejected the alleged subletting or parting with possession without consent. At L121, the court dismissed the petition because the petitioner failed to prove the necessary ingredients of section 14(1)(b). The absence of an established transfer explains why the court did not need to make a separate determination concerning written consent. However, this supports only the proposed contextual explanation, not the accompanying whole-premise classification of FALSE. The court did not affirmatively find that written consent existed, nor did it independently determine whether written consent had been withheld. That factual issue remains unresolved on the supplied source.

original_spans.original: Therefore, it cannot be said that it is the case of subletting or parting with possession without consent of the landlord.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The source confirms that the petitioners instituted eviction proceedings concerning the identified tenanted shop under Section 14(1)(b), among other grounds. The original petition expressly alleged sub-letting, assignment, or parting with possession. Record 1 establishes the subsequent Tribunal proceedings concerning that eviction claim, while the judgment's account of the original petition supplies the precise allegations. The connection is supported as procedural history and party pleading, not as proof that sub-letting actually occurred.

original_spans.original: That the respondent has already sub-letted, assigned and otherwise parted with the tenancy premises

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 2 and the underlying judgment support R1.P2 rather than oppose it. The High Court acknowledged Arun Sood's presence and simultaneous operation of Sood Stores, alongside the respondent's continuing business activity. These facts establish concurrent commercial use. They do not contradict the premise that such concurrent activity occurred. Although the evidence contradicts the separate allegation that the respondent had effaced himself from the shop, that allegation belongs to R1.P3, not R1.P2. The proposed opposition therefore targets the wrong premise and incorrectly assigns its whole-premise state as false.

original_spans.original: it also being not disputed that the son was engaged in the business of Sood Store which was run simultaneously from the premises

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 3 establishes continued occupation and business participation by Agya Ram Sood. This contradicts, rather than substantiates, the alleged exclusive occupation by Arun Sood. The High Court expressly found no evidence that the respondent had effaced himself from the tenanted shop and accepted corroborated evidence of the respondent's continuing occupation and business activity. Consequently, Record 3 cannot support R1.P3's proposition that evidence substantiated surrender of possession or control. The proposed connection reverses the evidentiary inference adopted by the High Court. The appropriate evidentiary conclusion is absence of proof of effacement, not proof of exclusive occupation by the son.

original_spans.original: the respondent- tenant continues to be not only in use and occupation of the premises but also engaged in the business run therefrom.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 directly reports that the Additional Rent Control Tribunal allowed the respondent-tenant's appeal against the Additional Rent Controller's eviction order. The Tribunal held that the petitioners had failed to prove sub-letting. The following paragraph confirms that the eviction order was set aside and the eviction petition on that ground was dismissed. This matches R2.P2 in procedural stage, appellate outcome, relevant statutory ground, and statement status. It is a correctly attributed appellate finding and order, without improperly treating failure of proof as proof that every factual allegation was false.

original_spans.original: it was held that the petitioners had failed to prove sub-letting.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed connection correctly identifies evidence undermining the landlords' allegation that M/s Gargson was originally the proprietorship of Om Prakash Gupta, but it materially overstates what that evidence establishes and mischaracterizes its relationship to the court's finding. PW1 admitted that Arun Kumar Garg had remitted and deposited rent as proprietor of M/s Gargson; he did not expressly admit that Arun Kumar Garg owned the concern at the inception of the tenancy. RW1 testified that Arun Kumar Garg conducted business under the Gargson name, but she also acknowledged that she could not produce documentary evidence establishing his proprietorship. The initial rent receipt did not identify Om Prakash Gupta as proprietor, and PW1 lacked personal knowledge of the original tenancy arrangements. The Tribunal therefore concluded that the appellants failed to prove their alleged original proprietary identity. This evidence supports, rather than directly opposes, the Tribunal's finding. The proposed connection additionally upgrades a failure of proof into an affirmative determination of original proprietorship. That upgrade is not supported by the judgment.

original_spans.original: Besides, the burden of proof was on the appellants to establish that the tenant inducted by their predecessor into the tenanted premises was the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta and not of Shri Arun Kumar Garg and that the said sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta had sublet or parted with possession of the tenanted shop to the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Arun Kumar Garg, both of which aspects could not be proved by the appellants during trial.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed connection accurately identifies the photographed Gargson Autoplast signboard and evidence of the concern's separate Najafgarh Road address as relevant to the unsuccessful subletting allegation. However, it mischaracterizes the evidentiary attribution and overstates the conclusion. The signboard's location was evaluated by the Tribunal from the appellants' photographs, not established conclusively through PW1's testimony. The Tribunal expressly questioned whether the depicted window belonged to the tenanted shop and assumed that location only for the sake of argument. Even on that assumption, the signboard did not establish subletting or parting with possession. The separate industrial-unit address was supported by exhibited documents Ex. RW1/6 and RW1/7, but evidence of operations at another address does not conclusively establish that Gargson Autoplast never possessed or used the tenanted premises. Moreover, the proposed connection describes the trial evidence as directly opposing the court's finding, although the Tribunal relied on its assessment of this evidence to uphold the dismissal of the subletting ground. The source supports failure to establish the alleged transfer, not an affirmative finding that subtenancy or occupation was impossible.

original_spans.original: it does not show that M/s Gargson sublet or parted with possession of the tenanted premises to M/s Gargson Autoplast.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The Supreme Court records that the genuineness of Kothandarama Ayyar's will was undisputed. The judgment independently reproduces paragraph 5, which grants Nagammal a life interest in Kothangudi and provides the remainder to Gnanambal and her children subject to the Rs. 5,000 payment to Alamelu. It also reproduces paragraph 13, which refers to Nagammal's enjoyment of Kothangudi as stated in paragraph 5. Although the linked record presents Gnanambal's position as a party claim, the testamentary text independently establishes the existence of both provisions. Their combined significance must be determined through construction of the will as a whole.

original_spans.original: the village of Kothangudi shall be enjoyed by Nagammal as stated in paragraph 5

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The judgment identifies Raju Ayyar as a son of the testator's nephews who was adopted by the widow under the will. The will expressly contemplated adoption of either a son of Gnanambal or a son of one of the testator's nephews. The actual adoption therefore fell within the second contingency, for which paragraphs 11 to 16 specified modifications to the earlier dispositions. Although the linked record concerns Raju Ayyar's pleaded claim, the adoption itself is independently recorded as an undisputed material fact.

original_spans.original: Raju Ayyar, who was a son of the testator's nephews and was taken in adoption by the widow in terms of the will

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed connection incorrectly treats the linked High Court finding as supporting the continued operation of paragraph 5. The High Court actually held that paragraph 5 did not operate when the widow adopted a nephew's son. Its interpretation was therefore contrary to the proposed connection. The Supreme Court subsequently rejected that interpretation and expressly held that paragraphs 11 to 16 did not change paragraph 5. Thus the substantive proposition is supported by the Supreme Court's adopted construction, but the specified SUPPORT relationship to the linked High Court record is incompatible with that record's meaning and judicial status. The historical disagreement was resolved on further appeal.

original_spans.original: paragraph 5 of the will did not come into operation at all.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: The testamentary text expressly provides that Nagammal would enjoy Kothangudi during her life and that the property would thereafter pass to Gnanambal and her children, subject to payment of Rs. 5,000 to Alamelu. The Supreme Court adopted the construction that paragraph 5 remained operative notwithstanding adoption of a nephew's son. This defeats Raju Ayyar's asserted entitlement based on an undisposed remainder. Although the linked procedural record states the final appellate result rather than independently setting out the testamentary entitlement, the Supreme Court's substantive reasoning and the reproduced will directly support the proposed connection. The judgment does not establish that the payment was actually made or separately determine its enforcement.

original_spans.original: No change is made in paragraphs 11 to 16 with regard to the provision in paragraph 5 of the will.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Raju Ayyar sued for possession of Kothangudi on the allegation that the remainder after Nagammal's life interest had not been disposed of and therefore passed to him as the adopted son and heir. The trial court dismissed his suit, and the High Court reversed that dismissal. The Supreme Court held that paragraph 5 remained operative, thereby defeating the pleaded inheritance basis. Its final order allowed Gnanambal's appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment and decree, and restored those of the Subordinate Judge. The connection accurately describes the appellate outcome without extending the judgment to separate questions of payment performance, individual rights of Alamelu's heirs, or ownership of unrelated properties.

original_spans.original: The result is that the appeal is allowed, the judgment and decree of the of the High Court are set aside and those of the Subordinate Judge restored.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 expressly prevents the Singhs from executing the decree or taking possession of the disputed land before satisfying the payment condition. This supports opposition to R2.P2, which asserts that the compromise itself created a present and immediate interest upon execution. The Supreme Court confirmed that the contemplated underlease was contingent and that its existence could not be determined before payment. This establishes the absence of an immediate interest at execution, without establishing whether payment occurred afterward.

original_spans.original: Until the payment was made it was impossible to determine whether there would be any under- lease or not.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 directly supports R2.P3 by identifying the payment obligation of Rs. 8,000 within two months and restricting execution of the decree and possession until payment. The compromise provisions and the Supreme Court's analysis establish that the contemplated underlease was conditional. This connection concerns the existence and legal effect of the condition, not whether the Singhs subsequently fulfilled it.

original_spans.original: The whole arrangement was made conditional on the Singhs paying Rs. 8,000 to Kumar within 2 months from the date of the compromise

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 supports R6.P1 because the compromise expressly required timely payment of Rs. 8,000, provided for cancellation if that requirement was not satisfied, and prohibited execution and possession before payment. These provisions establish the conditional nature of the Singhs' enforceable rights under the compromise. The connection correctly describes the decree's conditions without asserting that nonpayment actually occurred.

original_spans.original: Otherwise all the terms of the compromise Will stand cancelled and the plaintiffs shall not be competent to claim any right to or possession over the.land covered by the patta dated 11th March, 1921.

label: UNRESOLVED
basis: Record 4 establishes that the material issue before the Supreme Court was the admissibility of the unregistered compromise decree. The supplied judgment does not establish whether the Singhs actually paid Kumar Rs. 8,000 within two months of 6 March 1923. The record therefore supports identifying an evidentiary gap, but it does not supply affirmative evidence contradicting actual payment. The proposed opposition cannot be established as a factual negation of R6.P2. Whether the payment condition was satisfied remains unresolved.

original_spans.original: The only plea which is material for the purpose of this appeal is that the compromise decree not having been registered was inadmissible in evidence.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 2 reproduces the account of the sudden river-course change in Fasli 1341, but the passage at L123 belongs to the allegations reported from the plaint beginning at L120. It is not itself a trial-court factual finding. The Supreme Court independently adopts the occurrence and timing of the sudden change at L162, supporting the substantive truth of R5.P1. Nevertheless, that later appellate reasoning does not validate the proposed attribution of Record 2 to a trial-stage court finding. The connection improperly upgrades reported pleading content into an adjudicated fact.

original_spans.original: The allegations as they appear in the plaint

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 2 concerns the river's sudden departure from its former channel and movement outside the villages. The separate passage at L122 describes the disputed tract's location and the plaintiff's asserted possession before that change, within the account of the plaint. Neither passage establishes that the land retained its physical character and identity after the change. The Supreme Court expressly establishes that condition at L163. Thus R5.P2 is supported by the judgment, but the proposed connection incorrectly derives the condition from Record 2 and the earlier geographical description. The asserted implication is not sufficient evidence for the complete premise.

original_spans.original: the character and identity of the land have remained intact

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 3 expressly recognizes the plaintiff's entitlement to possession on the strength of original title under section 4(2). However, L163 does not independently explain the acquisition of that title through the earlier operation of Dhar Dhura. The specific explanation appears at L161, where the Supreme Court reasons that the land northwest of the former main stream had come to the plaintiff under the custom. The proposed connection therefore attributes the complete original-title acquisition reasoning to a record that states its resulting entitlement rather than its full historical and legal basis. Additionally, Record 3 is Supreme Court appellate reasoning, not a trial-stage finding as classified. R5.P3 is supported by L161 read with L163, but not by the proposed record-specific connection in its stated status, stage, and scope.

original_spans.original: the entire stretch of land lying to the north west of the main stream came to the plaintiff under the custom of Dhar Dhura.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: The proposed witness quotation is authentic but occurs at L162, not in Record 3 at L163. L162 expressly states that Dhar Dhura no longer governed the parties' rights after the river shifted beyond the village limits. L163 instead applies section 4(2) to the plaintiff's possession entitlement, relying on the sudden change and continued identity of the land. The Supreme Court's territorial analysis at L156-L159 independently supports the cessation of the custom's operation under those geographical circumstances. Consequently, R5.P4 is established elsewhere in the supplied judgment, but the proposed connection incorrectly attributes the express cessation finding to Record 3 and misclassifies Supreme Court appellate reasoning as a trial-stage finding.

original_spans.original: the custom of Dhar Dhura would no longer govern the rights of the parties

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: Record 1 supports the existence of a 999-year lease granted by the Trustees, a local authority, covering the land and completed building. However, R5.P1 specifically concerns the bidder's construction obligation as part of the contractual bargain preceding that lease. Record 1 does not independently establish that obligation. The proposed connection also substitutes the property-based interpretation of section 4(1), which belongs to R4.P1, for the contractual construction premise R5.P1. Furthermore, although Sitaram Luxman was the successful bidder and was declared tenant at the auction, the formal 1916 indenture was executed with Rustomji Dhunjibhoy Sethna, the receiver of his estate. Identifying the bidder without this distinction as the original recipient of that indenture is inaccurate. The construction obligation and the complete bargain are established separately in lines L125, L128, L130 and L131, but the proposed connection does not accurately relate Record 1 to its designated premise.

original_spans.original: one Rustomji Dhunjibhoy Sethna the receiver of the estate of Sitaram Luxman

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: R5.P5 expresses the deferred-vesting alternative: that the lessor would acquire ownership of the building for the first time only upon expiry, forfeiture or re-entry. The Supreme Court expressly rejected that proposition. Record 5 correctly reports the Court's finding that the lessor became the building's owner after its construction and retained ownership throughout the lease, subject to the lessee's contractual enjoyment. Consequently, Record 5 contradicts R5.P5 rather than supporting it. The proposed SUPPORT direction and whole-premise TRUE designation are incompatible with the designated premise and the appellate finding. The same record could support the rejection of R5.P5, but not the affirmative connection proposed here.

original_spans.original: Forfeiture does not, for the first time, give title to the lessor.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Records 1 and 5 support the material ownership connection to R3.P2. Record 1 establishes that the Trustees granted the lease of the land together with the completed building. Record 5 establishes the Supreme Court's appellate finding that the lessor owned the building notwithstanding the lessee's construction expenditure and contractual right of enjoyment. The source additionally establishes that the Trustees' property vested in the Bombay Municipality in 1925. The Court expressly determined that the demised premises, including the building containing disputed Block B/2, belonged to a local authority and were outside the operation of the 1947 Act. This supports R3.P2 at the required property-specific and appellate stages. There is a citation and chronology error in the proposal's supporting metadata: line L135 describes the Society's acquisition of the lessee's interest in 1948, not the Municipality's acquisition of the lessor's interest. Municipal succession is established by line L134. That error does not overturn the separately established substantive ownership connection.

label: SUPPORTED
basis: Record 5 establishes the Supreme Court's finding that the building belonged to the lessor rather than the lessee. This finding supplies the ownership determination required for the first-part exemption under section 4(1). The statutory text excludes premises belonging to Government or a local authority, and the Court expressly applied that exemption to the demised premises, including the building. The resulting statutory noncoverage directly supports R8.P1. The ownership finding and the Court's express conclusion together establish the proposed connection at the correct appellate stage. The exemption concerns these particular premises and is not a general exemption for every building constructed by a lessee.

original_spans.original: In' our view in the case before us the demised premises including the building belong to a local authority and are outside the operation of the Act.

label: UNSUPPORTED
basis: R8.P2 identifies the Society's ejectment proceeding against D. C. Patel concerning Block B/2 before the Bombay City Civil Court. Those procedural facts are established in the judgment, especially lines L135, L136 and L139. However, the proposed connection specifically attributes their establishment to Record 2. Record 2 concerns the lease covenants requiring repair, maintenance and rebuilding and reserving inspection and re-entry rights to the lessor. It does not identify the Society as plaintiff, Patel as defendant, Block B/2 as the disputed unit, or the City Civil Court as the forum of the ejectment action. The proposed connection therefore uses an incompatible record for R8.P2. The underlying procedural premise is true, but its asserted evidentiary connection to Record 2 is unsupported.
